newsitem.title: USA: Defective gene diminishes ovarian cancer threat.
newsitem.headline: Defective gene diminishes ovarian cancer threat.

text.p: Women with ovarian cancer are more likely to survive longer with the disease if they carry a defective form of the gene for breast cancer known as BRCA1, according to a study published in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.

The study "is the first to identify a difference in clinical outcomes of patients with altered BRCA1 genes and ovarian cancer," said Olufunmilayo Olopade, a researcher at the University of Chicago, in an editorial accompanying the study.

The normal form of BRCA1, even though it is often called the "breast cancer gene," actually protects against the development of a tumour by fixing defects in the DNA that would otherwise lead to cancer.
But when BRCA1 mutates and can no longer do its job effectively, the DNA defects go unrepaired and -- if the conditions are right -- cells grow uncontrollably, creating a tumour.

In an examination of 53 women with the defective gene conducted at research centres throughout the United States, Dr. Stephen C. Rubin and his colleagues found that even women with an advanced stage of ovarian cancer were likely to live longer on average than women who had a normal form of BRCA1.
Those with defective BRCA1 lived for an average of 6.5 years, as opposed to those with a normal gene who survived for a little over two years, researchers said.
"Cancers associated with BRCA1 mutations appear to have a significantly more favourable clinical course," the Rubin group concludes in the Journal.

Although defective BRCA1 genes are linked to "only a small proportion of ovarian cancers," the researchers said, looking for the gene appears to be the best method yet for gauging the fate of a woman with advanced ovarian cancer.
